candidates.decision_reason: Official payment-provider status incident directly connects checkout authentication failure to a firewall configuration change.
candidates.evidence_summary: AltaPay reported that 3-D Secure authentication in its Shopify embedded application stopped functioning correctly. Affected customers could not finalize credit-card payments at checkout. AltaPay traced the incident to a firewall configuration change. A mitigation restored payment processing, after which the team continued investigating the origin of the firewall change.
candidates.title: Credit Card Payment Failures on Shopify Embedded App

candidates.decision_reason: Vendor issue record directly describes database connections not being returned to the pool and resulting application unresponsiveness.
candidates.evidence_summary: Atlassian tracked a Crucible production bug in which the application became unresponsive after running for a period of time. The failure was attributed to BoneCP database connections not being returned to the pool, leaving database connections unavailable to the application. Restarting the application restored service temporarily, consistent with exhausted leaked pool state. Atlassian classified the issue as a major bug and fixed it in subsequent Crucible releases.
candidates.title: BoneCP connections are not returned to pool

candidates.decision_reason: Primary company postmortem explicitly documents unclosed database connections as a root-cause mechanism in connection-pool exhaustion; the multi-factor nature is preserved in the evidence.
candidates.evidence_summary: CoderDen reported a roughly 45-minute full platform outage in which API requests returned 503 errors. One of two explicitly identified root-cause mechanisms was an unclosed database query in a high-traffic endpoint. A missing rows.Close/defer path prevented PostgreSQL connections from being returned, causing connection leakage under load. Aggressive background scheduling compounded the exhaustion, so the candidate is scoped specifically to the documented connection-leak mechanism rather than claiming a single-cause incident.
candidates.title: SEV-1: Database Connection Exhaustion Incident

candidates.decision_reason: Primary production bug report isolates row-by-row related-record loading as an N+1 mechanism; the separate search-index problem is explicitly excluded from this mapping.
candidates.evidence_summary: A real self-hosted production Dify installation reported a roughly 740 GB PostgreSQL database, peak QPS around 100, and six API replicas. The ordinary first log page triggered per-row workflow_runs lookups, explicitly described as an N+1 pattern, with large TOAST fields deserialized for each row. The reporter validated that the page-1 base SQL itself was sub-millisecond and that the list-page cost came from row-by-row run-detail loading, decompression, serialization, and payload transfer. The same report also describes a separate unindexed keyword-search full scan; this candidate is intentionally scoped only to the ordinary list-page N+1 mechanism.
candidates.title: Log pages extremely slow on large DB: N+1 workflow_runs loading

candidates.decision_reason: Primary incident report attributes the outage to progressive memory exhaustion caused by an explicit slow memory leak.
candidates.evidence_summary: DNSimple reported a production outage in its San Jose region that made its redirector service unreachable. Its hosting provider identified a slow memory leak in a network switch, triggered by packets from monitoring checks becoming stuck. The leak eventually exhausted the switch memory and prevented it from processing incoming packets. The hosting provider planned a network-switch software upgrade specifically to prevent recurrence of the memory leak.
candidates.title: Incident Report - San Jose Region and Redirector Service Outage

candidates.decision_reason: Official status record explicitly resolves an apparent service degradation as a false alarm with no elevated errors.
candidates.evidence_summary: Fastly initially posted that it was investigating elevated Cloud WAF errors. Customer Incident Response later changed the event from degraded performance to available/informational after investigation. Fastly explicitly confirmed the status update was a false alarm and that there were no elevated Cloud WAF errors. Other locations and services were unaffected throughout the investigation.
candidates.title: (False Alarm) Cloud WAF Performance Issues

candidates.decision_reason: Official incident report directly attributes complete service loss to a database node filling its disk with WAL transaction logs.
candidates.evidence_summary: git.nrw reported a complete GitLab outage lasting 5 hours 45 minutes. Database replication had silently stopped, leaving one database node to accumulate WAL transaction logs. The remaining database node's disk filled with WAL logs and the service went down. The incident was resolved by increasing disk capacity and restoring replication, with WAL-size monitoring added as follow-up.
candidates.title: Incident: gitlab.git.nrw outage

candidates.decision_reason: Primary operational report directly traces a bounded PostgreSQL pool outage to connections not returned on stream teardown, with deterministic reproduction, pool-exhaustion evidence, restart recovery, and a negative control. The issue was closed only for template noncompliance.
candidates.evidence_summary: A checked-out PostgreSQL connection is not returned on live-stream teardown; the per-worker pool drains to 8/8, database-dependent requests time out or 504, the pool remains exhausted after streams end, and restart clears the leaked state.
candidates.title: PostgreSQL gevent-pool connection leak on live-stream teardown drains the per-worker pool

candidates.decision_reason: Firsthand production narrative matches the frozen N+1 failure mode and is pinned to an exact public Git repository state and source blob. The source has not yet been materialized into EvalForge's raw primary-source snapshot layer, so the candidate remains non-admitted.
candidates.evidence_summary: The backend engineer describes a production appointment endpoint that fetched patient details one-by-one for each appointment, explicitly calls the pattern a typical N+1 query problem, records 6,000+ database calls and about four seconds of latency for one doctor, and reports recovery after batching the patient lookup into one database call.
candidates.title: It Worked in Dev. It Worked in QA. Then Production Happened.

candidates.decision_reason: Primary production incident tracker explicitly concludes false alarm/no customer impact after a visible deployment-related distractor, matching the no_fault control semantics.
candidates.evidence_summary: GitLab opened an incident because production component versions appeared out of sync across zonal clusters after deployment. Investigation determined the condition was a false alarm caused by stale metadata for a ContainerStatusUnknown pod whose containers had already exited. No traffic was reaching the lingering pod and GitLab explicitly reported no customer impact. Deleting the stale pod cleared the alert; the visible deployment/version disparity was therefore a distractor rather than an active service fault.
candidates.title: GitLab Versions differ across zonal clusters

candidates.decision_reason: The official incident root-cause section directly identifies a payment configuration update as the trigger for failed credit-card payment processing, and rollback of that configuration resolved the failure.
candidates.evidence_summary: A production payment-configuration update intended for virtual credit cards prevented affected U.S. credit-card payments from processing until engineers rolled back the configuration change.
candidates.title: Payment configuration update prevented U.S. credit-card processing

candidates.decision_reason: The final official investigation states that the suspected ingestion incident had no service degradation and no supported CrowdStrike alerts were missed, making it a defensible real-world negative-control candidate for no_fault.
candidates.evidence_summary: An operationally visible suspected ingestion issue was investigated and the final supported-service finding was healthy: no service degradation and no supported CrowdStrike alerts missed.
candidates.title: Mandiant Managed Defense reported ingestion issue resolved as no degradation

candidates.decision_reason: Primary company incident report directly identifies a production memory leak as the trigger for repeated backend crashes and customer-visible errors.
candidates.evidence_summary: Honeycomb reported four roughly 20-minute ingest brownouts in which 1–3% of customer telemetry was rejected. The incident trigger was explicitly identified as a slow memory leak that accumulated over hours across ingest backends. The backends crashed within minutes of one another as memory pressure accumulated, causing in-flight and new ingest requests to fail. After the leak was identified, Honeycomb reverted the bad commit and deployed a fixed release; memory behavior and service health returned to normal.
candidates.title: Incident Report: Running Dry on Memory Without Noticing

candidates.decision_reason: Primary production database profiling explicitly identifies an N+1 query pattern, quantifies millions of repeated lookups, and points to batching as the fix.
candidates.evidence_summary: Production pg_stat_statements showed SELECT-by-key as the database's highest-volume query with 3,830,328 calls in the observation window. The existing batched equivalent accounted for only 134,057 calls, a reported 28:1 ratio of unbatched to batched lookups. The issue explicitly diagnoses pages that resolve list items individually as an N+1 pattern and recommends replacing loops with the existing get_many batching path. The repeated single-row lookups consumed roughly 2.5 million milliseconds of database time and increased cache/I/O pressure on the production database.
candidates.title: perf: N+1 queries on thing table causing 3.8M single-row DB lookups

candidates.decision_reason: The cited leaks are not established database-connection leaks and are not the primary incident root cause.
candidates.evidence_summary: The report mentions Kibana connection leaks during remediation, while the primary outage root cause is ZooKeeper coordination-layer instability and loss of quorum.
candidates.title: Elastic Cloud AWS us-east-1 outage of February 2019

candidates.decision_reason: Potential label match, but evidence is too thin to admit as a locked research incident without preserving the original source narrative.
candidates.evidence_summary: The pinned entry states only that a third-party-library memory leak caused two outages, without enough incident detail for family/evidence construction.
candidates.title: Skyliner outages on 2017-01-19 and 2017-01-23

candidates.decision_reason: The incident is billing-related and configuration contributed materially, but the causal chain is broader than the frozen broken_payment_configuration label.
candidates.evidence_summary: A network partition overloaded Redis; a restart then loaded an incorrect configuration/read-only state, after which auto-recharge repeatedly charged customers.
candidates.title: Twilio billing system incident of July 2013

candidates.decision_reason: Direct match to EvalForge's runtime resource-exhaustion memory_leak label.
candidates.evidence_summary: The incident narrative explicitly identifies an EBS data-collection-agent memory leak that slowly consumed system memory and degraded request handling.
candidates.title: AWS US-East Region Service Event of October 22, 2012

candidates.decision_reason: Keyword/title says memory leak, but it does not match EvalForge's resource-exhaustion memory_leak semantics.
candidates.evidence_summary: The root cause is a parser buffer over-read/pointer-boundary bug that disclosed memory contents, not progressive runtime memory consumption.
candidates.title: Cloudflare parser bug causes memory leak

candidates.decision_reason: Direct match to disk_exhaustion rather than a generic disk hardware/storage failure.
candidates.evidence_summary: A background-job log grew without bound until it filled the filesystem, causing critical writes to fail and the service to stop.
candidates.title: Tarsnap outage 2016-07-24

candidates.decision_reason: N+1 behavior was a separate contributing issue, so labeling the whole incident n_plus_one_query would overstate the evidence.
candidates.evidence_summary: The narrative reports an accidental N+1 database join, but identifies GKE Dataplane V2 anetd CPU saturation and packet drops as the persistent incident root cause.
candidates.title: GKE Dataplane V2 anetd CPU saturation causes connection timeouts

candidates.decision_reason: Primary engineering postmortem directly documents filesystem capacity exhaustion as the mechanism that stopped database progress and replication.
candidates.evidence_summary: SoundCloud described a production database outage in which maintenance activity generated more than 3 GB/minute of MySQL binary logs. The binlog partition expanded from roughly 10 GB to 100 GB of usage in about 30 minutes and then filled completely. The disk-full condition caused a partial binlog write, corrupted the final event, stopped slave replication, and left the master unable to make progress. Recovery required expanding the binlog volume and failing over to a consistent slave.
candidates.title: Doing the right thing

candidates.decision_reason: Official payment-platform post-incident report directly attributes checkout authentication failures to a configuration misconfiguration.
candidates.evidence_summary: Cybersource reported an incident affecting the Payer Authentication setup service on April 28, 2026. A configuration issue caused some authentication requests routed through one data center not to complete as expected. The root cause was a misconfiguration in the data center health-check mapping introduced during a prior change. Cardholders could see checkout errors or need to retry transactions; rollback/correction restored payer-authentication behavior.
candidates.title: Post-Incident Report: Payer Authentication Setup Errors
